objectives: Describe Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve + the savings method.
Explain the spacing + testing effects + desirable difficulties.
Compare Leitner, SuperMemo SM-2, half-life regression + modern SRS algorithms.

slides.title: Ebbinghaus + the forgetting curve
slides.body:
**Hermann Ebbinghaus** Über das Gedächtnis (1885; trans. Memory 1913): the founding experiment of memory science. Using himself as the sole subject + nonsense syllables (CVCs like ZOF, BIK) to neutralize prior meaning, Ebbinghaus measured how long it took to relearn a list at varying delays — the **savings method**.

**Savings**: if a list took 1000 s to learn originally + 400 s to relearn, savings = (1000-400)/1000 = 60%. The savings curve traces retention over time.

**The forgetting curve**: retention drops sharply in the first hour + day, then flattens. A common phenomenological model:

  R(t) = e^(-t/S)

where R is retention probability, t is elapsed time, + S is **memory stability** (sometimes 'memory strength'). Stability grows with successful review.

**Modern refinements** (Wixted, Carpenter):
- The curve is better fit by a **power function** than a pure exponential.
- Forgetting depends on encoding strength, retrieval practice, + the spacing of prior reviews.
- Each successful retrieval increases stability — the **stability-enhancing** effect.

**Ebbinghaus also discovered** (in the same monograph):
- **The spacing effect**: distributed practice beats massed practice for long-term retention.
- **The serial-position effect**: primacy + recency.
- **Overlearning**: rehearsing beyond perfect recall increases durability.

Ebbinghaus's work was largely solo + ignored for decades; rediscovered as cognitive psychology matured + remains the empirical bedrock of memory research.

slides.title: Spacing + testing effects + desirable difficulties
slides.body:
**The spacing effect** (Cepeda et al. 2006 meta-analysis; Bjork; Rohrer): distributed practice produces more durable + transferable learning than the same total time massed. The **optimal gap** scales roughly as ~10-20% of the desired retention interval — to retain for a year, review at ~1-2 month gaps; for an exam in a week, review across the week.

**The testing effect / retrieval practice** (Roediger + Karpicke 2006 'Test-Enhanced Learning' Psychological Science): act of retrieving from memory is itself a powerful learning event, more powerful than restudy. Their classic study: students who studied a text + then took a test outperformed students who restudied the text four times, especially at one-week delay. Karpicke + Blunt 2011 extended this — retrieval beat concept mapping even when students rated concept mapping as the better strategy.

**Mechanisms**: retrieval reconsolidates the trace, makes context cues more discriminative, + may strengthen multiple alternative routes to the memory. Retrieval-induced facilitation (Anderson, Bjork, Bjork) generalizes; retrieval-induced forgetting also exists.

**Interleaving** (Rohrer + Pashler; Taylor + Rohrer): mixing problem types within a session beats blocking by topic for **discrimination learning** — students learn not only how to solve a problem but how to choose the right method. Particularly powerful in mathematics + category learning. Feels less effective during practice (fluency illusion).

**Robert + Elizabeth Bjork — desirable difficulties** (1994+):
- Spacing.
- Interleaving.
- Variability of conditions.
- Generation (vs reading).
- Reduced + delayed feedback.
- Tests as learning events.

Difficulties that slow apparent performance but increase long-term retention + transfer. Inverse correlation between fluency + durability is one of the most counter-intuitive findings in the science of learning.

**Caveats**:
- For severe novices, difficulty must be calibrated — Sweller's CLT still applies.
- Spacing benefits depend on at least one successful retrieval before forgetting; very long gaps without scaffolding fail.
- Testing benefits are largest when retrieval is effortful but mostly successful (~80-90% success target in modern SRS).

slides.title: Spaced-repetition systems: Leitner → SuperMemo → modern
slides.body:
**The Leitner system** (Sebastian Leitner So lernt man lernen 1972): a paper flashcard system with several boxes; correct cards advance to a less-frequent box, incorrect cards return to box 1. First widely-used implementation of the spacing effect for self-study.

**SuperMemo + SM-2** (Piotr Woźniak; first software 1987; SM-2 algorithm published 1990 as part of his PhD work): the canonical spaced-repetition algorithm.

SM-2 sketch:
- Each card has interval I (days) + ease factor EF (≥ 1.3).
- Learner grades each recall on 0-5 (0 complete blackout; 5 perfect).
- If grade < 3: reset I to 1; do not change EF strongly.
- If grade ≥ 3: I_next = I_prev · EF (with I_1 = 1, I_2 = 6).
- EF updated: EF := EF + (0.1 - (5-q)·(0.08 + (5-q)·0.02)).
- EF capped below at 1.3.

**Anki** (Damien Elmes 2006+, open source): widely-used SM-2 derivative; powerful add-ons + media; large communities for languages, medicine (medical school flashcards), law.

**SuperMemo (later versions)**: SM-15, SM-17, SM-18 introduced **two-component model of memory** (stability S + retrievability R), neural-network-based interval optimization, + the **Algorithm SM-18** that fits per-user difficulty.

**Duolingo + half-life regression** (Settles + Meeder 2016 ACL): rather than a hand-tuned schedule, Duolingo fits a per-user, per-word model of memory half-life from log data:

  p(recall) = 2^(-Δ/h)

with half-life h regressed from features (word, lexeme, prior practice, errors). At scale, ML-optimized scheduling outperforms hand-coded SM-style heuristics.

**Quizlet Learn + Khan Academy + Babbel** + many platforms now integrate adaptive scheduling.

**Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler (FSRS)** (Jarrett Ye 2022+): open-source successor to SM-2; fits a three-parameter Difficulty, Stability, Retrievability model from user logs; default in modern Anki (Anki 23.10+). State of the art for open SRS.

**Modern frontier**:
- LLM-assisted card generation (LLM produces cards from textbook passages; user reviews).
- Mnemonic generation (Duolingo, mem.ai).
- Multimodal retrieval — images, audio, situated.
- Integration with metacognitive prompts + explanation tasks (active recall + elaboration).
- Personalized retention-target selection (FSRS lets users target e.g. 90% retention, trading review load for retention).

**Practical workflow**:
1. Make atomic cards (one fact each; the minimum-information principle, Woźniak).
2. Use cloze deletions for fragments + Q-A for relationships.
3. Maintain ~85-95% recall target; lower → too hard, higher → wasted reviews.
4. Combine SRS with spaced + interleaved problem practice for transfer.

question.question: Compute SM-2 interval growth
question.goal: A card has EF=2.5, currently at interval I=6 days. Learner reviews + grades it 5. Compute next interval + next EF; then re-review at the new interval with grade 4.

steps.reveal: I_next = 6 × 2.5 = 15 days. SM-2 multiplies the prior interval by the ease factor for grades ≥ 3.

hints: At q=5 the bracketed term is 0.1.
steps.reveal: For q=5: EF_new = 2.5 + (0.1 - 0·(...)) = 2.6. Ease grows on perfect recall, drifts down on weaker recall, floored at 1.3.

steps.prompt: After 15 days, grade is 4. Compute new EF.
steps.reveal: For q=4: EF_new = 2.6 + (0.1 - 1·(0.08 + 0.02)) = 2.6 + 0 = 2.6. (SM-2 treats q=4 as 'no change' near default ease.) Slight numeric variants depending on exact reference formulation.

I_next = 15 × 2.6 = 39 days. The interval roughly doubles each successful recall — the exponential schedule that approximates the forgetting curve. A failure (q < 3) would reset I to 1 + slightly lower EF.

question.question: What does Roediger + Karpicke (2006) demonstrate about test-enhanced learning?
options: Testing only measures learning; it does not produce it.

Retrieval practice itself is a powerful learning event. Their study compared studying a text four times vs studying then taking three free-recall tests; at five-minute delay, restudy looked better, but at one-week delay the test group substantially outperformed restudy. Retrieval restructures the memory trace, strengthens cues, + makes the knowledge more durable. The effect generalizes across materials (texts, vocab, anatomy, mathematics) + populations + is among the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology.
Testing harms learning by inducing anxiety.
Rereading + highlighting are superior because they feel easier.
question.explanation: Roediger + Karpicke 2006: retrieval beats restudy at long delays. Restudy looks better in immediate tests (fluency illusion) but retrieval produces durable learning. Generalizes broadly; basis of practice-testing recommendation in Dunlosky 2013.

hints: Restudy vs test groups; long-delay outcome.
Testing as learning, not just measurement.
slides.workedSolution: Roediger + Karpicke 2006 PSci: at five-minute delay restudy ≈ test; at one-week delay test >> restudy. Retrieval practice reconsolidates + strengthens memory traces, makes context cues more discriminative + produces durable + transferable learning.

question.question: Designing an SRS deck for a medical student
question.prompt: A first-year medical student wants to retain 2000 anatomy facts for their Step 1 exam in 18 months + for clinical practice afterward. Design an SRS workflow: card construction (Woźniak's minimum-information principle), scheduling target, mix with active problem solving + clerkships, + how you would monitor retention + review load over time.

question.question: Forgetting curve R(t) = e^(-t/S). With stability S = 20 days, retention after t = 7 days?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how spaced-repetition systems operationalize Ebbinghaus + Bjork's desirable difficulties.
question.rubric: Mentions: Ebbinghaus 1885 forgetting curve R = e^(-t/S) showed retention decays then plateaus; spacing distributes practice; testing effect (Roediger + Karpicke 2006) makes retrieval itself a learning event. Bjork's desirable difficulties — spacing, retrieval, interleaving, generation — slow apparent performance but build durable memory. Leitner 1972 paper boxes operationalized this; Woźniak's SM-2 (1990) scheduled reviews by I_next = I × EF with EF responsive to grades; Anki 2006 brought SM-2 to a wide audience; FSRS 2022 + Duolingo half-life regression fit per-user memory models from logs. Each successful retrieval at the edge of forgetting maximally grows stability — Bjork's principle implemented as an algorithm. Modern systems combine LLM-assisted card creation, multimodal review, + targeted retention thresholds (e.g., 90%) to balance review load against retention.
